description: Second Payment Services Directive. Harmonises regulation of payment services in the EU. Introduced strong customer authentication (SCA), open banking APIs (XS2A), and licensing for payment institutions and e-money institutions.

Proposed directive to replace PSD2. Published by Commission June 2023. Focuses on: enhanced fraud liability, IBAN name verification, access to payment systems, consolidated licensing. Legislative process ongoing.

Proposed directly applicable EU regulation accompanying PSD3. Transfers many current PSD2 directive provisions into a regulation for consistent application across Member States. Covers PSP obligations, liability, and user rights.

Regulation on information accompanying transfers of funds and certain crypto-assets (Travel Rule). Requires full originator and beneficiary information with wire transfers and crypto-asset transfers. Applies from 30 December 2024. No minimum threshold for crypto.

Entity authorised to provide payment services: credit institutions, e-money institutions, payment institutions, and post office giro institutions. PSPs are obliged entities under AMLR for payment services activities.
Authorised payment service provider that is not a credit institution or e-money institution. Licensed under PSD2/PSD3. Cannot hold customer deposits. Obliged entity under AMLR.

Institution authorised to issue electronic money and provide payment services. Regulated under E-Money Directive 2009/110/EC (EMD2). E-money is a substitute for coins/banknotes; subject to AMLR CDD obligations.

PSD2 mandates Account Servicing Payment Service Providers (ASPSPs) to provide access to account data and payment initiation to Third Party Providers (AISPs and PISPs) through secure APIs. AML implications: TPPs may introduce layering risk.

Authentication based on at least two of: something you know, something you have, something you are. Mandatory for electronic payments in the EU under PSD2 Art. 97. SCA interacts with AML transaction monitoring — SCA bypass is a fraud/ML typology.

PSD3/PSR proposal requires PSPs to verify that payee's name matches the IBAN before credit transfer execution. Addresses mismatch fraud and reduces money laundering via payee substitution. Implementation deadline still being determined.

canonical_name: Travel Rule — Wire Transfer and Crypto Information
description: TFR Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 requires originator's name, account number, address and beneficiary's name/account to accompany all fund transfers. For crypto-asset transfers: full originator and beneficiary information at ANY amount (no minimum threshold).

Payment service where funds are received from a payer and transmitted to a payee in another location, without any payment accounts being created. Specific AML risk: used for cross-border value transfer. Obliged entity under AMLR.

Natural or legal person acting on behalf of a payment institution in providing payment services. PI remains fully liable for agent's compliance. AML obligation: agents must comply with PI's AML framework. Agent registry maintained by NCAs.

PSD2 sets liability rules for unauthorised transactions: consumer bears max €50 unless PSP failed in security obligations. PSD3 proposes expanded PSP liability for APP (Authorised Push Payment) fraud where victim is deceived. AML intersection: APP fraud proceeds require ML.
PSD2 provisions on liability for unauthorised transactions, refund rights for direct debits, and obligations on users to notify PSPs of unauthorised transactions. Must notify PSP without undue delay.

Payment service providers of payers must ensure transfers are accompanied by: payer name, account number (IBAN/BIC), and payer address or official document number or DOB or customer ID. For crypto transfers: same information at any amount.

PSPs are obliged entities under AMLR in addition to PSD3/PSR obligations. CDD under AMLR applies to all PSP customers. TFR Travel Rule is a key intersection point. PSP agent AML obligations flow through AMLR.

TFR Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 is the implementation of FATF Recommendation 16 (Wire Transfers) and R.16's crypto extension. TFR Art. 4 and AMLR Art. 83 are complementary. Crypto CASP Travel Rule obligations sit at TFR × AMLR intersection.

TFR requires collection and transmission of personal data (originator/beneficiary). GDPR applies to this processing. TFR provides the legal basis (legal obligation) for GDPR Art. 6(1)(c). Data retention periods must comply with both TFR and GDPR.

PSPs must implement SCA for: initiating electronic payment transactions, accessing payment accounts online, and remote payment operations. Exemptions available (low-value, low-risk, merchant-initiated). RTS on SCA issued by EBA.

PSP and CASP process for TFR compliance: collect originator information at payment initiation; transmit with payment; intermediary PSPs must pass through information; beneficiary PSP must detect missing/incomplete information and take appropriate action including SAR if necessary.

EBA issues binding technical standards and guidelines on PSD2/PSD3: SCA RTS (EBA/RTS/2017/02), agents and outsourcing guidelines, complaints handling, and operational/security risk guidelines. Also issues opinions on open banking implementation.

Third party provider with access to payment account information. Licensed under PSD2/PSD3. AML risk: AISP data access could be abused. AISPs are not full payment service providers but have data processing obligations.

Third party provider that initiates payment orders from a user's payment account held at another PSP. Licensed under PSD2/PSD3. AML risk: PISP-initiated payments may bypass traditional AML controls. Subject to AMLR as payment service provider.
